mcqs.question: Orders, Inventory, and Payments are deployed as three separate services, but all three read and write the same shared database. What is the main consequence?
options: The services aren't actually independent — any team can silently break another team's queries by changing a shared column
There is no consequence, since the services still deploy on separate schedules
The shared database automatically enforces consistent APIs across all three services
This setup improves failure isolation compared to separate databases
mcqs.explanation: A shared schema means any team's change can silently break another team's queries with no compiler or API contract catching it, which is the real coupling that undermines independence — separate deploy schedules don't fix that. A shared database enforces no API consistency on its own, and it actually weakens failure isolation since all three services depend on the same database's health.

mcqs.question: A dashboard needs a fast, frequently-run query joining order and customer data that's split across two services' databases. Which approach is the better fit, and why?
options: API composition, calling both services live for every dashboard load, since it requires no new infrastructure
A CQRS read model built ahead of time from events, since it avoids repeated live cross-service calls for a query that needs to be fast and frequent
A shared database migration, merging both services back into one schema
Neither — cross-service queries should never be supported
mcqs.explanation: For a query that's frequent and needs to be fast, a pre-built CQRS read model (kept in sync via events) avoids the repeated live round-trips that API composition would require. API composition works for occasional, low-volume lookups but isn't the better fit here; merging services back reintroduces the shared-database coupling problem, and cross-service queries are a normal, supportable need.

mcqs.question: A team needs strong, immediate consistency across two entities, and only one team owns both. Based on the shared-DB vs database-per-service trade-off, what's the reasonable default?
options: Database-per-service, because it is always the correct choice for any two entities
A shared database (or one service's schema) is fine here, since strong consistency matters and there's no cross-team coordination cost to avoid
Neither — both entities should be stored only in a cache
CQRS should be used regardless of the consistency requirement
mcqs.explanation: When one team owns both entities and needs strong, immediate consistency, a shared schema (or single service) avoids paying an eventual-consistency cost for no autonomy benefit, since there's no second team to protect from schema coupling. Database-per-service is not a universal default, storing only in a cache doesn't address consistency across entities, and CQRS is a solution to a query-performance/autonomy problem, not a requirement regardless of consistency needs.

mcqs.question: A new Shipping service is given direct read access to the Orders table "temporarily, just to ship faster." Six months later, it's still reading that table directly. What is the most likely reason this became permanent?
options: Direct table access turned out to have no real downsides, so there was no reason to change it
The Orders team lost the ability to modify their own schema entirely
Removing the workaround requires coordinated cross-team work with no urgent forcing function, so it never gets prioritized
Shipping's queries automatically migrated to a proper API once the schema stabilized
mcqs.explanation: Workarounds like this tend to persist because fixing them requires coordinated effort across teams with no urgent trigger forcing the work, even though the coupling cost (Orders can't freely change its schema) keeps accruing silently. It's not that the access is harmless, Orders doesn't lose modification rights outright (it just risks breaking Shipping silently), and nothing automatically migrates the query to a proper API.
